new_statements.quote: Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length) Stress is predictable and usually falls on the final syllable.
new_statements.citation: Colich, Kim. 1995. Tami Organised Phonology Data. Ukarumpa: SIL (SIL Language & Culture Archives item 42454), 4 pp.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (4 pp., text layer, PDFMaker 2004, author Kim Colich). extracted text of PDF page 3 gives exactly: "Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)" / "Stress is predictable and usually falls on the final syllable." - verbatim as quoted, at the stated locator. The sheet is a standard SIL Organised Phonology Data form: inventory, consonant/vowel example lists, this one-line suprasegmental section, syllable patterns (V, VV, VC, C [syllabic nasal], CV, CVV, CVC), orthographic conventions, a transcribed Luke 2 passage. No example is stress-marked, no secondary stress, no exceptions given, so the primary reader's rule_in_words / secondary_stress / exceptions fields are accurate. Reading fixed: fin…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and falls, as a rule, on the last syllable of the word.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the hedge 'usually'; no exceptions are listed and no example is stress-marked. Note the conflicting older second-hand statement in Schmidt 1900: 373 (based on Bamler's 1890-93 manuscript / Bamler 1900): 'Der Accent liegt im Allgemeinen auf der vorletzten Silbe' (accent generally on the penultimate syllable). Schmidt also notes that Tami has lost almost all original final vowels, which may be relevant to the penult-vs-final discrepancy but neither source says so.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, phonemic/orthographic data sheet; no discussion of phrase-level prominence or of citation vs connected forms. The source is a 4-page SIL Organised Phonology Data sheet (first-hand SIL fieldwork, data checked by Colich, Sept. 1995), not a full phonology.
new_statements.identity_note: Same language as tami1290 / ISO tmy. Colich 1995 gives the data location as Malasiga, Morobe Province (villages Tamigidu, Malasiga, Wanam, Kalal), i.e. the mainland-coast Tami settlements; OLAC lists alternate names Taemi, Wanam. Schmidt 1900 / Bamler 1900 describe the speech of the Tami (Cretin) Islands themselves plus the adjacent coast between Langemak Bay and Cape Cretin. No dialect split is named in either source.

readall_conflicts: Ross 1988 adds nothing, so the catalog's final-syllable reading (Colich 1995 OPD, p. 3: 'Stress is predictable and usually falls on the final syllable') stands as the best-supported modern statement. The disagreement already held by the project for this language remains: Schmidt 1900 (ZAOS 5: 373, based on the missionaries' 1890-93 manuscript and Bamler 1900) says 'Der Accent liegt im Allgemeinen auf der vorletzten Silbe' (penultimate), which contradicts Colich's final placement; Ross 1988 does not arbitrate, since it cites Bamler 1900 only as the sole sketch of Tami and makes no prosodic claim.
